name: external-configuration-store
context: Applications ship with configuration baked into deployment packages — files on disk, resource bundles, build-time constants — so changing an endpoint, a feature flag, or a batch size requires a rebuild and redeploy of every instance. That produces three failures at once: configuration changes are coupled to code releases, instances running different code can hold different settings during a rolling deploy, and the same connection string or theme has to be re-declared in every application that needs it. The External Configuration Store pattern moves configuration out of the deployment artifact into a centralized, versioned store that applications read at runtime, so behaviour can change without a release. Azure names the two responsibilities separately: routine settings (feature flags, endpoints, business parameters) belong in the configuration store, while secrets (connection strings, API keys, certificates, passwords) belong in a dedicated secret-management system and are referenced from the store — putting credentials in the config store turns a config change into a credential leak. The store also has to solve the derived problem: an application that fetches its config from the network on every request has traded a restart for a runtime dependency, so nearly every real implementation pairs the store with a local cache plus change notification or polling for invalidation.
benefits: Configuration changes take effect without a rebuild, redeploy, or restart, removing config edits from the release pipeline
One artifact runs unmodified across dev, test, staging, and production because all environment-specific values are supplied at runtime
Settings are shared across applications instead of duplicated — a queue URL or schema version is defined once
Rolling deploys stop producing mixed-configuration windows, because instances converge on the same store rather than carrying divergent local files
Change history and audit become a property of the store rather than of the version-control log: point-in-time recovery, immutable snapshots, and progressive rollout of a setting
Feature flags stop being compile-time constants, enabling canary rollout and runtime kill switches without a code change
Typed and labelled configuration surfaces let the store validate a setting's schema before it reaches an application
One place to review 'what is configured where', replacing grep across N config files
tradeoffs: The store becomes a runtime dependency and a new shared single point of failure; if it is unreachable and the local cache is cold or expired, the application cannot start or must fall back to baked-in defaults
Requires an availability and latency plan of its own — geo-replication, availability zones, and a bounded staleness budget for the local cache
Configuration becomes live mutable state, which destroys the property that code is immutable and reviewed: a one-line setting change can alter production behaviour without a peer review of code
Shared settings create blast radius across applications — an administrator editing one key can break every consumer, because nobody can reason locally about who reads a shared key
Typed configuration surfaces are versioned schemas, and a schema change is a breaking change for every consumer, reintroducing the coordination coupling the pattern was meant to remove
Observability and debugging get harder: the effective behaviour of an instance is now the composition of its binary version and whatever the store returned at read time
Operational cost of running and patching a config service, and the temptation to put too much into it until it becomes a second database with schema migrations
use_cases: Feature flags and kill switches toggled without redeploying the service that reads them
One immutable container image promoted across dev, staging, and production with environment values injected at runtime
Shared endpoints — queue URLs, service base URLs, downstream API hosts — defined once for a family of applications
Tenant-specific limits and overrides served per tenant from a multi-tenant SaaS control plane
Configuration rollback after a bad settings change, using the store's revision history and point-in-time recovery
Progressive rollout of a new setting value to a percentage of instances before it goes to all of them
Edge and IoT workloads receiving configuration pushed by a cloud controller with local caching for intermittent connectivity
avoid_when: Requirements are genuinely static — there is nothing to change after deploy, so the store is pure overhead
The application is a single small service with a handful of settings and no fleet to keep in sync
You cannot yet operate a highly available shared service and would be trading a restart for an outage
Secrets are the only thing being stored — use a secret manager with references, not a config store holding credential values
Independent deployment of the config schema from the consuming code is not actually achievable in your platform, so the store just becomes a deployment artifact with extra hops
Regulatory requirements demand that every effective configuration is captured in a signed, immutable release artifact rather than read at runtime
component_types: Configuration Store: the centralized, versioned backing system holding key/value settings — cloud key-value storage, a dedicated config service, or a hosted database
Configuration Client / Library: the in-process component that reads settings, exposes them as typed values, and hides store access from application code
Local Cache: an in-memory copy so the steady-state read path does not hit the network; the store or client implements cache-aside and tolerates store unavailability
Change Notification Channel: the push or poll mechanism that invalidates the cache so a setting change propagates without a restart
Revision / Snapshot Store: immutable history plus point-in-time recovery, so a bad change can be rolled back without redeploying
Access Control and Identity: managed identity plus role-based access rather than connection strings, with private endpoints for network isolation
Configuration Authoring / Rollout Controller: the component that stages a new value to a subset of instances before promoting it
anti_patterns: Config store used as a secret vault — connection strings and API keys stored directly as settings instead of referenced from a dedicated secret system
Store with no local cache, turning every settings lookup into a network hop and coupling application latency to store latency
Boot-time-only read: configuration is fetched at startup and never refreshed, so the store is an indirection with none of the benefit of live reconfiguration
One giant shared namespace where every team writes every key, making it impossible to reason about who breaks when a value changes
Config changes applied straight to 100% of instances with no staged rollout, converting a settings edit into an untested production deploy
Store treated as a general-purpose database — mutable business data accumulates until schema migrations and locking problems appear
Fallback to silently baked-in defaults when the store is unreachable, hiding a broken dependency behind plausible-looking behaviour
design_principles: Configuration is data, not code: settings changes must not require a build, so they are governed with the same review and staging discipline as deployment
Separate settings from secrets: routine configuration in the store, credentials in a dedicated secret system, store entries holding only references
Local cache with bounded staleness: never make the store a per-request dependency, and make the cache's expiry window an explicit, agreed budget
Version everything: keep revisions, point-in-time recovery, immutable snapshots, and per-environment labelling so a bad value can be undone
Fail open to a known-good value: an unreachable store must degrade to last-known-good cached configuration, never to an empty or invented setting
Typed configuration with schema validation: expose settings as typed values and reject a malformed or wrongly-typed change at write time, not at application start-up
Least exposure: private endpoints, managed identity, and role-based access rather than long-lived connection strings, because the store is reachable by every workload
best_practices: Provision the store in an availability-zone-supported region and geo-replicate, so clients read from the nearest replica and can switch during a regional outage
Keep secrets in a secret manager and store only a reference; use managed identity and RBAC to authenticate applications instead of connection strings
Expose configuration to Kubernetes workloads through a provider that renders ConfigMaps and Secrets, rather than baking a client into every container
Push configuration changes through the same staged, tested pipeline as code changes, and canary a new value before promoting it
Use content type and label metadata so the store returns a value the application already knows how to parse
Prefer a push-based refresh or short poll interval over fetch-on-read, and log which revision an instance booted with
Give the store the same availability SLO as the application tier it configures, and alert on cache-miss rate and store latency
